```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(psych) # Omega
library(lavaan) # CFA analysis
library(mirt) # IRT analysis
library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges) # ridgeline plot
library(ggcorrplot) #corrplot
library(paletteer) # color palette
library(flextable) # table in APA
```

```{r}
data = read.csv("International_vaiak.csv")
```

# Introduction

In the following report, I will discuss the results of the analyses carried out on the Art Interest (AI) scale of the VAIAK.

The AI scale is composed by 11 items. These are either about subjective interest (e.g., I am interested in art) or behaviors (e.g., I go to visit art exhibitions). Each item is rated on a 7-point Likert scale. Items of subjective interest are rated from “not at all” (1) to “very much” (7), while behavioral items range from “less than once a year” (1) to “once a week or more often” (7). Only one scale is consider, and no subscale is measured.

You can find the content of the items [here](#items).

Only participants who have completed the complete scale are taken into account.

# Sample

```{r}

data_ai = data %>%
  filter(
    if_any(AI_1_1:AI_2_4, ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
  mutate(
    Expertise = ArtExp_Expertise_cluster) %>%
  mutate(
    interest_subj = rowSums(across(AI_1_1:AI_1_7)), 
    interest_beha = rowSums(across(AI_2_1:AI_2_4)))

```

`r nrow(data_ai[data_ai$Dem_Age < 18, ])` participants were under the age of 18, so I excluded them.

```{r}

data_ai = data_ai %>%
  filter(Dem_Age >= 18 | is.na(Dem_Age))

```

The final number of participants is `r nrow(data_ai)`, with an average age of `r round(mean(data_ai$Dem_Age, na.rm = T), 2)` years, $sd$ = `r round(sd(data_ai$Dem_Age, na.rm = T), 2)`. For `r nrow(data_ai[is.na(data_ai$Dem_Age),])` participants we did not have the age. For the gender the sample is composed by `r nrow(data_ai[data_ai$Dem_Gender == "Female", ])` women, `r nrow(data_ai[data_ai$Dem_Gender == "Male", ])` men and `r nrow(data_ai[data_ai$Dem_Gender == "Other", ])` people that define themselves neither as woman or man.

Many participants were lay people (N = `r sum(data_ai$Expertise == "Lay person", na.rm = TRUE)`) with an important number of art experts as well (N = `r sum(data_ai$Expertise == "Expert", na.rm = TRUE)`). For the majority we do not have the expertise level (N = `r nrow(data_ai[is.na(data_ai$Expertise),])`).

```{r}

data_ai_score = data_ai %>%
  count(Art_Interest, name = "n") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Art_Interest))

```

The following graph represent the distribution of the score, the line is the mean (`r round(weighted.mean(data_ai_score$Art_Interest, data_ai_score$n), 2)`). The AI ranges from 11 to 77.

```{r}

N = sum(data_ai_score$n)                         # total number of participants
m = weighted.mean(data_ai_score$Art_Interest, data_ai_score$n)

ggplot(data_ai_score, aes(y = n, x = Art_Interest)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.9, 
           fill= MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese")[1], alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_void() +
  xlab("AI score") + 
  ylab("Frequency") +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray70", size = 1), 
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 18), 
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18, angle = 90), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        legend.position = c(0.20, 0.7),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14)) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = m,
    linetype = "dashed", 
    size = 1) +
  ggtitle(sprintf("Art Interest distribution")) 

```

## Internal reliability

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
omega_ai = data_ai %>%                              # Omega analysis Art Interest
  select(starts_with("AI")) %>%
  omega
```

McDonald's $\omega$, which is considered acceptable when above .7, was calculated and show a good internal reliability ($\omega$ = `r round(omega_ai$omega.tot, 2)`).

## Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)

For the CFA, I will keep in mind that a good fit is usually judged as such when the following criteria are respected:

-   CFI \> .9
-   TLI \> .9
-   RMSEA \< .8
-   SRMR \< .8

### One factor model

The first model tested is the one factor model with the two additional residual correlations based on prior studies.

![](images/Art%20interest%20model.png){fig-align="center" width="428"}

```{r}
Model_AI_one = "interest  =~ AI_1_1 + AI_1_2 + AI_1_3 + AI_1_4 + AI_1_5 + AI_1_6 + AI_1_7 +
                       
                           AI_2_1 + AI_2_2 + AI_2_3 + AI_2_4

                           AI_1_3 ~~ AI_1_7
                           AI_2_2 ~~ AI_2_4" 

AI_onefactor = cfa(Model_AI_one, data = data_ai, std.lv=TRUE, estimator = "MLR")  # CFA with MLR

table_cfa_one = fitMeasures(AI_onefactor, c(
  "chisq",
  "df",
  "pvalue",
  "cfi",
  "tli",
  "rmsea",
  "rmsea.ci.lower",
  "rmsea.ci.upper",
  "srmr"))    # Indices

table_cfa_one = as.data.frame(
  as.list(round(as.numeric(table_cfa_one), 4)))

names(table_cfa_one) = c("χ²", "df", "p", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "low RMSEA", "up RMSEA", "SRMR")

# APA style table

flextable(table_cfa_one) %>%
    autofit() %>%
  theme_apa() %>%  # APA-style formatting
  italic(part = "header", j = c("χ²", "p")) # italics 
```

The CFI, TLI and SRMR indicate a good fit, while the RMSEA is above the mentioned criteria.

Thus, I present the factor loadings ($\lambda$), which I judged keeping the general rule of thumb that a factor loading higher than .70 is excellent and above .50 is good.

```{r}

# Extract factor loadings, SE and p value 

loadings_one = parameterEstimates(AI_onefactor, standardized = TRUE) %>%
  filter(op == "=~") %>% # Filter only factor loadings
  select(
    Item = rhs,
    Loading = std.all,
    p = pvalue, 
    Variance = est) %>%
  mutate(
    R2 = Loading^2, 
    p = ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", as.character(round(p, 4))))

# Extract mean and SD 

item_names = as.character(loadings_one$Item)

item_data = data_ai %>%
  select(all_of(item_names))

content = c("School classes", 
            "Talking about art",
            "Art interested friends", 
            "Art interest", 
            "Motivation for art", 
            "Everyday art experience", 
            "Art interested family", 
            
            "Museum visits", 
            "Art books",
            "Art  reproductions", 
            "Art events")

descriptives = data.frame(
  Item = loadings_one$Item,
  Content = content,
  Mean = colMeans(item_data, na.rm = TRUE),
  SD   = sapply(item_data, sd, na.rm = TRUE))

# Unite the table

table_data = descriptives %>%
  left_join(loadings_one, by = "Item") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 4)))

# APA style table

flextable(table_data) %>%
  set_header_labels(
    Item = "Item",
    Content = "Content",
    Mean = "Mean",
    SD = "SD",
    Loading = "λ",
    R2 =  "R²",
    p = "p", 
    Variance = "Residual") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  theme_apa() %>%  # APA-style formatting
  italic(part = "header", j = c("Mean", "SD", "Loading", "R2", "p")) # italics 
```

We can also visualise the factor loadings to have a clearer view of the index. The two lines represents the two thesholds above mentioned to judge the factor loadings (0.5 and 0.7)

```{r}
table_data = table_data %>%
  arrange(desc(Loading)) %>% # to give the order
  mutate(Item = factor(Item, levels = Item)) # for ggplot

ggplot(table_data, aes(y= Item, x = Loading)) +
  geom_col(linewidth = 1.2,
           fill = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese")[4], 
           alpha = 0.8) +
  xlim(0, 1) +
  xlab("Factor loadings") + 
  ylab("") +
  ggtitle("Factor loadings of the AI items") +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray70"), 
        axis.text = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1)
```

All the items are above .5, but we can notice 6 items below .7: AI_1_1, AI_1_3, AI_1_7, AI_2_1, AI_2_2, AI_2_4.

Exploring the correlation of the residuals help us understand better the reason.

```{r}
residuals = residuals(AI_onefactor, type = "cor") # residuals

residuals = residuals$cov 

residuals[lower.tri(residuals, diag = TRUE)] = NA

residuals = residuals[,
  rev(colnames(residuals))]

ggcorrplot(residuals,
           lab = TRUE, 
           lab_size = 4,
           tl.cex = 12,
           digits = 2,
           show.diag = TRUE,
           ggtheme = theme_void,
           hc.order = FALSE,
           outline.color = "black", 
           colors = c(MetBrewer::met.brewer("OKeeffe1")[c(1, 6, 10)]))  +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    limits   = c(-0.3, 0.3),
    midpoint = 0) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"), 
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"))
```

We can notice that the items AI_2 have higher positive residual correlations compared to other items.

### Two factors model

As discussed in the prior months I proposed a different model, where the two parts of the scale are two separate factors (subjective interest and behavioural interest) with a hierarchical higher factor (art interest). This is motivated not only from theoretical discussion priorly carried out, but also on the analysis on the correlation residuals above.

![](images/Art%20Interest%202%20factors.png){fig-align="center" width="337"}

```{r}
Model_AI_two = "interest_subj =~ AI_1_1 + AI_1_2 + AI_1_3 + AI_1_4 + AI_1_5 + AI_1_6 + AI_1_7

                interest_beha =~ AI_2_1 + AI_2_2 + AI_2_3 + AI_2_4 

                interest =~ interest_subj + interest_beha" # model

AI_twofactor = cfa(Model_AI_two, data = data_ai, std.lv=TRUE, estimator = "MLR")  # CFA with MLR

table_cfa_two = fitMeasures(AI_twofactor, c(
  "chisq",
  "df",
  "pvalue",
  "cfi",
  "tli",
  "rmsea",
  "rmsea.ci.lower",
  "rmsea.ci.upper",
  "srmr"))    # Indices

table_cfa_two = as.data.frame(
  as.list(round(as.numeric(table_cfa_two), 4)))

names(table_cfa_two) = c("χ²", "df", "p", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "low RMSEA", "up RMSEA", "SRMR")

# APA style table

flextable(table_cfa_two) %>%
    autofit() %>%
  theme_apa() %>%  # APA-style formatting
  italic(part = "header", j = c("χ²", "p")) # italics 
```

The indexes all improved.

I again report here the table with the indices for each item.

```{r}

loadings_two = parameterEstimates(AI_twofactor, standardized = TRUE) %>%
  filter(op == "=~") %>% # Filter only factor loadings
  select(
    Item = rhs,
    Loading = std.all,
    p = pvalue, 
    Variance = est) %>%
  mutate(
    R2 = Loading^2, 
    p = ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", as.character(round(p, 4))))

# Extract mean and SD 

item_names = as.character(loadings_two$Item)

item_data = data_ai %>%
  select(all_of(item_names))

content_two = c("School classes", 
            "Talking about art",
            "Art interested friends", 
            "Art interest", 
            "Motivation for art", 
            "Everyday art experience", 
            "Art interested family", 
            
            "Museum visits", 
            "Art books",
            "Art  reproductions", 
            "Art events", 
            
            "Subjective Interest", 
            "Behavioural Interest")

descriptives = data.frame(
  Item = loadings_two$Item,
  Content = content_two,
  Mean = colMeans(item_data, na.rm = TRUE),
  SD   = sapply(item_data, sd, na.rm = TRUE))

# Unite the table

table_data_two = descriptives %>%
  left_join(loadings_two, by = "Item") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 4)))

# APA style table

flextable(table_data_two) %>%
  set_header_labels(
    Item = "Item",
    Content = "Content",
    Mean = "Mean",
    SD = "SD",
    Loading = "λ",
    R2 =  "R²",
    p = "p", 
    Variance = "Residual") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  theme_apa() %>%  # APA-style formatting
  italic(part = "header", j = c("Mean", "SD", "Loading", "R2", "p")) # italics 
```

The plot below shows the improvement of the factor loadings between the one factor and two factors model.

```{r}
table_data_combined = left_join(table_data, table_data_two, by = "Item") %>%
  arrange(desc(Loading.x)) %>%
  select(c("Item", "Loading.x", "Loading.y")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Loading.x, Loading.y),
    names_to = "Dataset")%>%
  mutate(
    Dataset = recode(Dataset,
                     "Loading.x" = "One factor",
                     "Loading.y" = "Two factors"))

ggplot(table_data_combined, aes(y = reorder(Item, -value), x = value, fill = Dataset)) +
  geom_col(
    position = "dodge",
    width = 0.7,
    alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese")[c(4, 6)]) +
  xlim(0, 1) +
  xlab("Factor loadings") + 
  ylab("") +
  ggtitle("Factor loadings of the AI items") +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray70"), 
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black")) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1)
```

Here as well all the factor loadings have improved, with AI_1_7 and AI_1_1 still below .7.

This in general make sense: Item AI_1_1 may be problematic because not everywhere they have art classes. Additionally certain classes may have art history classes (e.g., Italy) while other may have art classes where students create art. Item AI_1_7 asks how much once own family is interested in art, which as discussed elsewhere does not seem to be as strong as other items in describing the interest of the person.

## Item Responce Theory (IRT)

I carry out two distinctive IRT. One for the entire scale, the other with the two subfactors (interest_subjective and interest_behaviour) divided.

### One factor model

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
AI = data_ai %>% 
  select(starts_with("AI"))

AI_grm = mirt(AI, 1, itemtype = "graded") # run the model

coef = coef(AI_grm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE) # item parameters
```

This graph represent how informative on average the items are in relation to the ability of the participants ($\theta$).

```{r}
theta = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1000)

test_info = testinfo(AI_grm, Theta = theta)/ncol(AI)

df = data.frame(
  theta = theta, 
  information = test_info)

ggplot(df, aes(x = theta, y=information)) +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray70", size = 1), 
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 18), 
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18, angle = 90), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        legend.position = c(0.20, 0.7),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.background = element_rect(
          color = "black",  
          linetype = "solid")) +
  ylim(0, 4) +
  xlab("Theta") + 
  ylab("Test Information") +
  ggtitle("Information x ability for Art Interest") +
  geom_line(color = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese")[1], linewidth = 2)
```

We can notice that it is in general pretty normally distributed around 0, with a little skewness into the lower values. This means that it is more informative for the people with lower ability.

For each item, $a$ represents the discrimination parameter, i.e. how much the value vary in relation to the ability $\theta$. A high $a$ means that the probability of answering an item correctly changes very sharply as $\theta$ increases.

$b$ represents how much ability $\theta$ the participants needs to pass from a responce (e.g. 1) to the next (2). For example, in AI_1_1 a participant with an ability of least 0.08 (b5) has a 50% probability of responding 6 or higher. The higher the $b$ the more difficult it is for a participant to give that answer.

```{r}
coef_item = coef$items

plot_data = data.frame(
  item = rownames(coef_item),
  a = coef_item[, 1]) %>%
  arrange(desc(a)) %>% # to give the order
  mutate(item = factor(item, levels = item)) # for ggplot

table_data_irt = data.frame(
  Item = rownames(coef_item),
  Content = content,
  coef_item)

# APA style table

flextable(table_data_irt) %>%
  set_header_labels(
    Item = "Item",
    Content = "Content") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  theme_apa() %>%  # APA-style formatting
  italic(part = "header", j = c("a", "b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5", "b6")) # italics 
```

We can visualize the informativity of each item ($a$) also graphically.

```{r}
ggplot(plot_data, aes(y= item, x = a)) +
  geom_col(linewidth = 1.2,
           fill = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese")[1], 
           alpha = 0.8) +
  xlim(0, 5) +
  xlab("Item Discrimination") + 
  ylab("") +
  ggtitle("Discrimination parameter of the AI items") +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray70"), 
        axis.text = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"))
```

We can observe than the items already signaled before (AI_1_1 and AI_1_7) are the ones with the lower $a$. At the same time, all the items from the AI_2 are also on on the lower parts of the graph.

The following graph represents the $a$ and $b$ for each item and each answer. Each box is an item and each line represents the probability to answer in a specific way (P1 probability to answer 1). The slope of the lines represent the $a$, the steeper it is, the higher $a$ is, the more efficient is the question in distinguish between individuals who know the material and those who do not.

```{r}
p = plot(AI_grm,
         type = "trace",
         facet_items = TRUE,
         col = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese"), # color 
         lwd = 2, # size of the lines 
        auto.key = list(
          space = "right",
          columns = 1,
          cex = 1),
         par.strip.text = list(cex = 1), # size of the title box 
         par.settings = list(
           axis.text = list(cex = 1), # axis size
           par.main.text = list(cex = 1.4), # main title size
           strip.background = list(col = "grey90"), # backgorund color  
           strip.border = list(col = "black") # border around the strip 
         ))

p + latticeExtra::layer({ # add the grid 
  panel.grid(h = -1, v = 0, col = "grey85", lty = 1)   # horizontal grid only
  panel.abline(v = 0, col = "black", lty = 3, lwd = 1) # line at theta = 0
}, under = TRUE)
```

### Two factors model

Given that the two factors showed a better fit, I also tested an IRT by analysis the two subscales separately.

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
AI_subj = data_ai %>% 
  select(starts_with("AI_1"))

AI_grm_subj = mirt(AI_subj, 1, itemtype = "graded") # run the model

coef_subj = coef(AI_grm_subj, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE) # item parameters

coef_subj = coef_subj$items

test_info_subj = testinfo(AI_grm_subj, Theta = theta)/ncol(AI_subj)

df_subj = data.frame(
  theta = theta, 
  information = test_info_subj, 
  Dataset = "Subjective")
```

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
AI_beha = data_ai %>% 
  select(starts_with("AI_2"))

AI_grm_beha = mirt(AI_beha, 1, itemtype = "graded") # run the model

coef_beha = coef(AI_grm_beha, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE) # item parameters

coef_beha = coef_beha$items

test_info_beha = testinfo(AI_grm_beha, Theta = theta)/ncol(AI_beha)

df_beha = data.frame(
  theta = theta, 
  information = test_info_beha,
  Dataset = "Behavioural")
```

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
df_combined = bind_rows(
  df_subj,
  df_beha)
```

```{r}

ggplot(df_combined, aes(x = theta, 
                        y=information, 
                        color = Dataset)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 2) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese")[c(2, 4)]) +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray70", size = 1), 
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 18), 
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18, angle = 90), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.background = element_rect(
          color = "black",  
          linetype = "solid")) +
  ylim(0, 4) +
  xlab("Theta") + 
  ylab("Test Information") 
```

The behavioural scale seems to be more informative for the participants with a greater interest.

We can see in the following table the new indices for each items divided into two scales: subjective interest


```{r}

        auto.key = list(

          cex = 1),
         par.strip.text = list(cex = 1), # size of the title box 
         par.settings = list(

           par.main.text = list(cex = 1.4), # main title size
           strip.background = list(col = "grey90"), # backgorund color

}, under = TRUE)
```

and behaviorual interest

```{r}

table_data_irt = data.frame(
  Item = rownames(coef_beha),
  Content = content[8:11],
  coef_beha)

# APA style table

flextable(table_data_irt) %>%
  set_header_labels(
    Item = "Item",
    Content = "Content") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  theme_apa() %>%  # APA-style formatting
  italic(part = "header", j = c("a", "b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5", "b6")) # italics 
```

```{r}
p = plot(AI_grm_beha,
         type = "trace",
         facet_items = TRUE,
         col = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese"), # color 
         lwd = 2, # size of the lines 
        auto.key = list(
          space = "right",
          columns = 1,
          cex = 1),
         par.strip.text = list(cex = 1), # size of the title box 
         par.settings = list(
           axis.text = list(cex = 1), # axis size
           par.main.text = list(cex = 1.4), # main title size
           strip.background = list(col = "grey90"), # backgorund color  
           strip.border = list(col = "black") # border around the strip 
         ))

p + latticeExtra::layer({ # add the grid 
  panel.grid(h = -1, v = 0, col = "grey85", lty = 1)   # horizontal grid only
  panel.abline(v = 0, col = "black", lty = 3, lwd = 1) # line at theta = 0
}, under = TRUE)
```

We can also visualise the improvement of $a$ by comparing the index in the one factor model and the two factors model.

```{r}

coef_combined = rbind(coef_subj, coef_beha)

plot_data_two = data.frame(
  item = rownames(coef_combined),
  a = coef_combined[, 1]) %>%
  arrange(desc(a)) %>% # to give the order
  mutate(item = factor(item, levels = item)) # for ggplot

plot_data_combined = left_join(plot_data, plot_data_two, by = "item") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(a.x, a.y),
    names_to = "Dataset",
    values_to = "a")%>%
  mutate(
    Dataset = recode(Dataset,
                     "a.x" = "One factor",
                     "a.y" = "Two factors"))

ggplot(plot_data_combined, aes(y= item, x = a, fill = Dataset)) +
  geom_col(
    position = "dodge",
    width = 0.7,
    alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = MetBrewer::met.brewer("Veronese")[c(1, 3)]) +
  xlim(0, 5) +
  xlab("Item Discrimination") + 
  ylab("") +
  ggtitle("Discrimination parameter of the AI items") +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray70"), 
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 18, color = "black"))
```

This results seem in line with the one for the full scale, with the item AI_1_7 always having the lowest slope $a$.
